title: Welcome to Three Flows Solutions
imageAlt: Four hands fit green, yellow, blue and pink jigsaw pieces together on a white table.
recap: Every business is the management of three flows. Our job is to help you master all three — by teaching you what we know, and working beside you when knowing isn’t enough.

title: Four Ways to Cut Your Import Cost in a Tariff War
imageAlt: Stacked shipping containers in long rows fill a port yard, seen from above.
recap: Four legitimate, widely underused mechanisms can dramatically reduce what you pay to bring goods into the US. Most growing brands miss most of them.

title: The Real Cost of Factory Data Problems
imageAlt: Workers in blue coats assemble and pack small parts at a row of benches in a factory.
recap: The physical goods move. The paperwork doesn’t. Here’s what poor factory data quality actually costs growing brands — and what to do about it.

title: How Your Freight Gets Into Amazon's Warehouse
imageAlt: The Amazon logo with its orange smile arrow, mounted on the light-grey facade of a large warehouse above the employee entrance.
recap: What actually happens between the truck arriving at the dock and your listing showing “In Stock” — and how to keep your freight moving through it.

title: What the One Big Beautiful Bill Means for Your Business
imageAlt: A document headed 'ONE BIG BEAUTIFUL BILL' in white serif capitals, bearing the Great Seal of the United States, resting on an American flag beneath a metal clipboard clip.
recap: The most common mistake is treating these provisions as items to note and revisit at tax time. The value — especially on the R&D side — is in the planning before the filing, not in the filing itself.

title: Amazon's Two New Policies: What They Mean for Sellers
imageAlt: A laptop screen showing the Amazon website open in the Safari browser, with the Amazon logo, a "Deliver to Australia" label, and navigation links including Today's Deals, Customer Service, and Gift Cards.
recap: Within weeks of each other, Amazon announced two platform changes that quietly shift the ground beneath sellers. Neither is catastrophic on its own — but together, they reward sellers who already have their operations in order.

title: Where Should Your Third US Warehouse Be? A Case Study
imageAlt: A satellite night-lights view of the continental United States, where dense clusters of city lights mark population centres and the mountain west appears largely dark.
recap: A $180M home goods brand had climbing inventory costs and slower deliveries. Here’s what our Supply Chain Analyzer and Optimizer found, and the network we recommended.

title: Make or Buy, Local or Overseas: A Sourcing Question
imageAlt: A market stall table draped in black cloth displays rows of small round containers in pink, blue, and grey on wooden crates, with a framed sign reading "homemade" at the centre.
recap: A practical framework for small business owners just getting started — the 2×2 that covers most of the decision, and what to do when the theory meets reality.

title: Is a $2 or a $20 Product Better for Your Business?
imageAlt: A taped cardboard shipping box sits on a woven rug striped in yellow, blue, tan, and red.
recap: A quick unit economics walk-down, the "free shipping" trap, and how to tell whether a product is worth your time to sell.

title: Cashflow: What Unit Economics Doesn't Tell You
imageAlt: A white ceramic piggy bank on a green background, with three coins suspended in a line above its coin slot.
recap: A follow-up to the unit economics post — because a healthy per-unit P&L can still put you deep in the hole before you see your first dollar back.

title: FedEx's 5.9% GRI: What the Heat Map Reveals
imageAlt: A FedEx delivery truck parked on a snow-covered street during heavy snowfall, framed by bare winter trees.
recap: The headline rate increase is 5.9%. The actual distribution across weights and zones tells a different story — and every business owner should know how to see it.

title: Setting Up a Company: Plan Before You Act
imageAlt: A stencil reading 'Live, Work, Create' spray-painted in white on a red brick wall.
recap: Filing the paperwork takes an afternoon. The decisions that determine whether you filed the right thing take longer — and skipping that planning step is the single most common mistake founders make.

title: Why Google Workspace Is Enough to Start
imageAlt: Five illustrated people stand and sit on isometric tiles, each bearing a coloured Google app icon including Gmail, Calendar, Drive, and Play.
recap: Cash is tightest when the temptation to spend is strongest. One monthly subscription — seven to ten dollars — buys a professional foundation, and leaves the rest for the only job that matters this early: finding customers.

title: Is e-Commerce Too Late to Start?
imageAlt: An Amazon 4-star store sign mounted under the glass canopy of a shopfront entrance.
recap: Too late is the wrong question. E-commerce has not closed — it has stopped being free, and what it asks now is one real advantage: a product, an audience, inventory on hand, capital, a partner, or your own effort.

title: Sell Fast or Sell High: A Livestream Selling Model
imageAlt: A smartphone and a tablet mounted on tripods face a living room, the tablet running a live video switching app with a grid of source thumbnails beside a red countdown panel reading 4:42, and a lit Christmas tree blurred behind them.
recap: A client wanted to know two things before his first livestream sale: how low his price can go, and how fast he has to sell. It turned out neither question has an answer on its own.

title: Website Is Your Business Card. How Do You Make One?
imageAlt: A Times Square street at night lined with illuminated theatre and storefront signs, with cars and pedestrians at the crosswalk below.
recap: The first thing a customer checks is your website. Building one yourself teaches you more about your business — and in 2026, it no longer takes a developer.

title: Nike’s $2M Warehouse Theft: Nothing Was Hacked
imageAlt: Three people in red jumpsuits and matching Salvador Dalí masks pose together on a crowded city street at night, one holding a phone overhead.
recap: Twelve people were indicted in July over $2 million of Nike product that left a Memphis warehouse on 3,119 shipping labels. Nothing was hacked. The only fake thing was a sticker.

title: It's not only about Iran's gas price
imageAlt: A fuel pump display in Iran showing 1,500 per unit, 30.00 liters, and a 45,000 sale total.
recap: Someone posted a photo from a gas pump in Iran, and the comments filled with people trying to work out the price in dollars per gallon. Almost nobody could.
